title: What the guarded media fetch refuses, and under which code
pins: Which URLs `fetchPublicUrlContent()` refuses, and under WHICH CODE, in every language. The code is the contract — a consumer switches on it to decide whether to widen an allow-list, surface a hard stop, or report an SSRF attempt. The message is deliberately not pinned: the three implementations word these differently on purpose, and a test over the prose holds every language to a translation and reddens on a wording improvement that changed nothing. Same decision as `browser-url-policy`, and the same spellings — `private_address_refused` is one finding with one name across the ecosystem.
scope: The refusal decision of the OPT-IN guarded fetch and its code. It does NOT cover the unguarded `fetchUrlContent()`, which is unguarded by design in all three languages and must stay that way — url-0009 is the row that would redden if a language ever quietly guarded it. It does not cover what happens to bytes once a URL is admitted, and it is not a claim that a guarded fetch is safe: a name can resolve differently between the check and the request, which only connection-level pinning closes.
findings: Writing this corpus is what produced the codes it compares. The PHP guard originally threw plain exceptions carrying prose, so there was nothing for a consumer to branch on and nothing a port could agree with except wording. Fixed in particle-academy/prism 07f842b before the first row was recorded. The ports have NEITHER the guard nor the codes yet (G-63), so this suite is deliberately RED on two of three columns: it is the failing corpus the ports get built against, rather than a description of them written after the fact. Read a future green narrowly — this corpus compares languages, so a hole all three share would look exactly like agreement, which is why every row here is a hostile input and url-0001 is the only well-behaved one.

discrimination.note: url-0001 fetches successfully and url-0009 proves the UNGUARDED path still fetches a loopback address. A guard that refused everything would pass every refusal row and fail both of these.

ts.note: G-63: prism-ts has the unguarded fetch and no guarded variant.

py.note: G-63: prism-py has the unguarded fetch and no guarded variant.
